# Morning memo — 2026-09-20

**Source failures (if any):** none reported in this run. Note: 40 items claimed, 24 deferred by per-source volume caps, 16 scored. Most lobsters/hn items arrived with empty body content, so scoring leaned on title plus independent verification for the two public picks.

## Worth attention

- **Android 17 QPR1 adds new APIs without publishing them to AOSP** — https://grapheneos.social/@GrapheneOS/117282080803799576
  GrapheneOS reports Android 17 QPR1 is the first release since the 3.x era where Google shipped new developer APIs without the implementation landing in AOSP; the APIs are Pixel-only and September platform patches are being withheld from other OEMs until QPR2 in December 2026. GrapheneOS has a working QPR1 port it cannot ship and is backporting Pixel firmware and HALs instead. If you ship anything Android-adjacent, treat "new API in the docs" as no longer equal to "available in AOSP" and check availability per-distribution before you depend on it.

- **typesafe-computer-use: macOS computer-use agent for roughly $0.0002 per step** — https://github.com/awlevin/typesafe-computer-use
  An open source macOS agent that skips sending screenshots to a frontier model entirely: it OCRs the screen deterministically, uses a small classifier to pick the next action, and only calls a writing model when a text field genuinely needs free text. The author claims roughly 155x cheaper and about 20x faster than a frontier vision loop. Directly relevant to the MCP/agent work — worth reading the action-classification approach even if you do not adopt the repo, because the pattern (deterministic screen read + cheap classifier + selective LLM call) transfers to any computer-use loop where per-step cost is the binding constraint.

- **OpenAI overbilled for hosted containers in the Agent API** — https://status.openai.com//incidents/01M2VA7X37P1ASADSNZ1CG4N4D
  A billing defect caused higher-than-expected charges for OpenAI-hosted containers in the Agent API on 2026-09-18 (roughly a 20-minute window, now resolved). OpenAI says it is reviewing affected usage and preparing refunds. If you ran Agent API container workloads that night, check the usage dashboard rather than assuming the refund finds you.

- **Typst makes big strides** — https://lwn.net/Articles/1092993/
  LWN coverage of recent progress in Typst, the Rust-based typesetting system positioned as a faster, saner LaTeX alternative. Relevant if you generate PDFs or formatted documents programmatically — compile times and a scriptable model are the pitch. Not urgent; file under "evaluate next time the document pipeline annoys you."

- **I don't like passkeys** — https://hawksley.dev/blog/i-dont-like-passkeys
  A skeptical walkthrough of passkey UX and portability problems from a developer's perspective. Worth reading before committing a product to passkey-only auth, since the friction described lands on your support burden, not the spec authors'. Opinion piece, not data.

- **Benchmarking Wild vs Mold** — https://davidlattimore.github.io/posts/2026/09/18/benchmarking-wild-vs-mold.html
  Link-time benchmarks comparing the Wild linker against Mold from Wild's author. Narrow but concrete if you have a Rust or C++ build where link time is the inner-loop tax. Read the methodology before trusting the numbers — author is not neutral.

results.title: Android 17 QPR1 adds new APIs without releasing them to AOSP
results.summary: GrapheneOS reports that Android 17 QPR1 is the first release since the Android 3.x era in which Google added new developer APIs without publishing the implementation to AOSP. The new APIs are Pixel-only, and September platform patches are being withheld from other OEMs until Android 17 QPR2 in December 2026. GrapheneOS has a completed QPR1 port it cannot ship and is backporting Pixel firmware, drivers and HALs instead. If you build anything Android-adjacent, stop treating 'documented API' as 'available in AOSP' and verify per-distribution availability before depending on it.
results.raw_claim: Android 17 QPR1 is the first Android release since 3.x to ship new developer APIs whose implementations were not published to AOSP, leaving them Pixel-exclusive until QPR2 in December 2026.
results.uncertainty: Claim originates from GrapheneOS and secondary press coverage; Google has not published a direct statement confirming the withholding or its intended duration.
results.worth_mentioning_reason: A structural change in how Android platform code reaches non-Pixel devices, with direct consequences for API availability assumptions and security patch timing.
results.verdict_reason: Concrete platform-governance change with corroborating coverage; changes how developers should verify API availability and patch timing.

results.title: typesafe-computer-use: macOS computer use at roughly $0.0002 per step
results.summary: An open source macOS agent that drives the machine toward a plain-English goal without sending screenshots to a frontier model. It OCRs the screen deterministically, uses a small classifier to choose the next action, and only calls a writing model when a text field genuinely needs free text. The author claims roughly 155x cheaper and about 20x faster than a frontier vision loop, at about $0.0002 per step. Worth reading the action-classification pattern even without adopting the repo, since it transfers to any computer-use loop where per-step cost is the binding constraint.
results.raw_claim: typesafe-computer-use performs macOS computer-use automation for roughly $0.0002 per step by combining deterministic screen OCR with a small action classifier instead of sending screenshots to a frontier vision model.
results.uncertainty: Cost and speed multipliers are the author's own benchmarks; task success rate versus a frontier vision loop on non-trivial goals is not independently established.
results.worth_mentioning_reason: Directly applicable architectural pattern for cheap agent automation, and per-step cost is the main blocker for running computer-use loops at volume.
results.verdict_reason: Open source release with a reusable cost-reduction pattern that maps directly onto agent and MCP work.

results.title: OpenAI overbilled for hosted containers in the Agent API
results.summary: A billing defect caused higher-than-expected charges for OpenAI-hosted containers in the Agent API on 2026-09-18, in a window of roughly twenty minutes, now marked resolved. OpenAI says it is reviewing affected usage to identify impacted customers and prepare refunds. If you ran Agent API container workloads that night, check your usage dashboard rather than assuming a refund reaches you automatically.
results.raw_claim: OpenAI confirmed a billing defect that overcharged customers for OpenAI-hosted containers in the Agent API on 2026-09-18 and is preparing refunds for affected accounts.
results.uncertainty: The magnitude of overcharge and whether refunds are automatic or require a support request are not stated in the incident notice.
results.worth_mentioning_reason: Direct financial exposure for anyone running Agent API containers, with a concrete action: verify the invoice rather than trusting the automatic refund.
results.verdict_reason: Real cost exposure with a clear action, but the window was short and the incident is already resolved, so scope is narrow.

results.title: I don't like passkeys
results.summary: A developer-side critique of passkey UX, portability and recovery problems. Worth reading before committing a product to passkey-only authentication, because the friction described lands on your support burden rather than on the spec authors. Opinion rather than data, so treat it as a checklist of failure modes to test, not as a verdict on the technology.
results.raw_claim: A developer argues that passkeys introduce UX, portability and account-recovery problems that make them a poor sole authentication method for consumer products.
results.uncertainty: Item captured without body content; the specific objections raised were not verified, and the piece is explicitly opinion.
results.worth_mentioning_reason: Auth architecture is a decision that is expensive to reverse, and the support-cost angle is underweighted in most passkey advocacy.
results.verdict_reason: Relevant to a costly, hard-to-reverse auth decision, but it is opinion without data and applies only to products choosing passkeys.

results.title: Benchmarking Wild vs Mold
results.summary: Link-time benchmarks comparing the Wild linker against Mold, written by Wild's own author. Concrete and narrow: useful if you have a Rust or C++ build where link time is the inner-loop tax, irrelevant otherwise. Read the methodology before trusting the numbers, since the author is not a neutral party.
results.raw_claim: Wild's author published benchmarks comparing link times for the Wild linker against Mold.
results.uncertainty: Benchmarks are authored by the maintainer of one of the two tools being compared; independent replication was not checked.
results.worth_mentioning_reason: Build-loop latency compounds across every working day, and linker choice is a cheap change with measurable effect.
